confirmed.statement: Assignment happened per person, at consent, before the writing tasks. The paper calls the design 'a standard 2 × 2 between-subjects study design' and says in its limitations 'we employed a between-subjects design'. Each participant wrote all four tasks in one condition, and the paper says it could not capture what AI-condition participants 'would have written without AI suggestions'. So unit = individual and structure = between are right, and check (e) on within-person order does not apply.
confirmed.locator: p. 4, Section 3.3.1; p. 3, Section 3.1; p. 15, Section 5.4; p. 13, Section 4.4.3

confirmed.statement: Country was recruited, not assigned. The authors chose the US and India for their cultural distance from the model, and 'initially launched the study in India and allowed the participant count to stabilize before extending the study to the same number of participants in the US.' Only the AI condition was randomized, within each country. This matches what_was_assigned.

What was assigned is AI help on the participant's own writing, not a change in whose output is scored. AI-condition participants did a tutorial and then wrote in a textbox that 'fetched an inline autocomplete suggestion from GPT-4o if the user paused typing for 100 ms.' The similarity and classifier outcomes use embeddings of the essays the participants wrote.

The tool is generative AI. Suggestions came from 'OpenAI’s latest language model at the time, GPT-4o', with the essay topic embedded in the prompt. The codebook's scope names writing suggestions built on language models, so this is not an out-of-scope predictive keyboard. ai_tool.name_model = OpenAI GPT-4o and role = suggestions are right.

Section 4 repeats 65 AI participants, 36 in India and 29 in the US. The printed degrees of freedom fit these sizes: 4 x 53 - 2 = 210 and 4 x 65 - 2 = 258 essays in the type-token tests, and 2784 + 4 x 36 x 29 - 2 = 6958 cross-culture pairs (this check's arithmetic).

confirmed.statement: No count at assignment is printed, so n_randomized = null is right. Two rules define the analyzed sample, and both act after assignment. Participants 'had to complete both parts to complete the study and receive payment', and the team 'retained only those participants who were born in and had lived their entire lives in the same country', checked with the survey taken after the tasks. The paper gives no number who started, quit, or were dropped. The form's exclusions note covers the second rule but not the completion requirement. Neither changes randomized = yes.

The Indian split is uneven (24 No AI, 36 AI) and the US split is even (29, 29). The paper gives no allocation ratio and no reason for the split. Under simple 1:1 assignment, a split at least as uneven as 24 of 60 has an exact two-sided binomial probability of 0.155 (this check's computation, not the paper's). So the split does not undercut the claim of random assignment. Unreported non-completion after assignment could also produce it.

summary: The PDF supports every part of the assignment, arms, and ai_tool coding: it says four times that each participant was randomly assigned to write with inline GPT-4o autocomplete suggestions or without any AI (pp. 2, 3, 4, and 15), in a between-subjects design with country recruited rather than assigned, and Table 1 gives 24, 29, 36, and 29 analyzed participants (p. 3). The gaps leave criterion 1 intact: the paper gives no randomization procedure, allocation ratio, or count at assignment, and it analyzes only participants who finished both parts and passed the born-and-lived rule, so the 24 vs 36 Indian split (exact two-sided binomial probability 0.155 under 1:1 assignment) has no stated cause.
